newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel warns Syria it can meet any challenge.
newsitem.headline: Israel warns Syria it can meet any challenge.

text.p: Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai, in interviews on Sunday ahead of the Jewish Day of Atonement, warned Syrian President Hafez al-Assad that Israel was strong enough to meet any challenge.

"We have no interest in a war with Syria, rather in real negotiations with them, that they should be as intensive as they can be," Mordechai told Israel's newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth ahead of Yom Kippur, the holiest day of the Jewish year.

"And permit me to pass via you a warning to Syria and to Assad: Mr Syrian President, the State of Israel and its security forces are strong and able to fulfil their goals. On that I have not a speck of doubt. My advice to you is: Come, let us go a different path," he added.

Syria's recent redeployment of about a third of its 35,000 troops in Lebanon caused war jitters in Israel, where memories of an attack against it on Yom Kippur 1973, by Syria and Egypt run deep. Yom Kippur, during which Israel grinds to a halt and Jews fast, starts on Sunday night and runs for 25 hours.

"Yes, 23 years ago we were surprised. Our best people fell in the war. With our blood and bodies we stopped the enemy flood and brought victory to Israel, but with that we paid an awful and dear price," Mordechai, a former general, told Israel Radio.
Asked his assessment of the probability of war, he said:

"In my opinion the probability of war in the short term is not high. In the long term, events, deteriorations, external or internal situations can have an influence, always a possiblity like that exists and therefore we train...and do all the operations demanded."

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had said the redeployment, in which some of the Syrian troops moved to within striking distance of a key Israeli position on the Golan Heights, was an attempt to pressure Israel to make concessions on the strategic plateau it captured from Syria in 1967. Netanyahu said last week the situation was "under control".
Syrian Information Minister Mohammed Salman, in the first public word by a Syrian official on the redeployment, was quoted on Sunday as saying Netanyahu's "threats" spurred the move.
No peace talks have been held between Israel and Syria since Netanyahu, who rejects trading occupied land for peace, won Israel's May elections. Syria demands the return of the Golan.
Israel's Jerusalem Post newspaper quoted the commander of the U.N. Disengagement Observer Force on the Golan (UNDOF) as saying there had been no unusual activity in his area.
"On the Golan areas as such, there is no buildup of troops, no buildup of tension," Major-General Johannes Kosters said.
